did_you_know.text: The tribe of Manasseh was split into two halves — one half lived east of the Jordan with Reuben and Gad, the other half held territory inside Canaan.
The decision for east-of-Jordan settlement goes back to earlier books (see Numbers 32), where Reuben and Gad asked for land there and Moses set conditions.
Bashan, mentioned here, corresponds largely to today’s Golan Heights — a fertile area historically known for good pastures and strong bulls.
Shiloh, where the assembly met, was the central sanctuary and tabernacle site before the Jerusalem Temple existed.
Phinehas son of Eleazar was Aaron’s grandson; he appears earlier in the narrative and is associated with priestly office and zealous action against idolatry.
The warning about "your daughters" echoes the Baal‑Peor episode, where relations with Moabite women led to idolatry and a deadly plague.
Achan son of Zerah is cited as an example of a private sin that brought national anger; his theft is connected to Israel’s defeat at Ai in Joshua 7.
By invoking the divine names they call God as witness — a formula that gives their statement a legal, solemn character.
The idea of a "witness altar" is biblical: stones, pillars or altars were often used as physical signs and witnesses of agreements and boundaries.
The priests and leaders who accompanied Phinehas show that the priesthood acted as mediators and authorities in public disputes, not only as ritual officials.
The altar’s name, 'Witness', emphasizes its role as a sign to future generations that these tribes shared the same God even though they lived apart.
